screens.title: Cache Coherence Protocols in Detail
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll build a clear, practical understanding of cache coherence protocols used in shared-memory multiprocessors. You will learn the MESI protocol's four states, how processor reads and writes trigger state transitions, and how bus transactions such as BusRd, BusRdX and BusUpgr coordinate consistency. We'll also examine MESIF's forwarding optimization and MOESI's Owned state, both designed to reduce memory traffic by enabling cache-to-cache transfers or allowing a dirty copy to be shared. As you follow the chapter, you'll see concrete examples of state transitions, observe the coherence traffic produced by simple read-write sequences, and practice a short simulation comparing MESI and MOESI. Understanding these mechanisms matters because coherence traffic often becomes a performance bottleneck in multicore systems. By the end, you'll be able to reason about when a forwarder or an owned copy saves time and when BusUpgr avoids unnecessary data movement. Which part of the protocol do you expect will make the largest difference in your workloads?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you should be able to implement MESI state transitions, explain and compare MESIF and MOESI, and analyze coherence traffic for common access patterns. First, you will learn to map processor reads and writes to state changes and the bus operations they trigger, which is essential to reason about correctness and performance. Second, you will understand MESIF's forwarding and MOESI's Owned state and when each reduces memory input and output. Third, you will be able to trace cache-to-cache transfers and count bus transactions for a sequence of operations, identifying where writebacks occur. Finally, you'll apply these skills to a short simulation that contrasts MESI and MOESI and shows how an Owned state can eliminate writebacks during sharing of modified data. These objectives are practical: they let you predict when memory controller load grows and how protocol choices change latency. Think of these skills as tools you can use to evaluate architectures or tune software sharing patterns to reduce coherence overhead.

screens.title: MESI: The Four Fundamental States
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define each MESI state and connect it to correctness and performance. Modified means the cache line has been changed and memory is stale; this cache is the sole valid source. Exclusive means the cache has a clean copy and no other cache has it — the cache can promote to modified without notifying the bus. Shared means the line is clean and may be present in multiple caches; after a write, those other copies must be invalidated. Invalid means the line is not valid locally. These four states let caches avoid unnecessary traffic: E allows a write without a bus transaction, and S lets multiple readers avoid coordination. A concrete example: a core that reads a block and then writes it alone will often get E and then go to M with no bus traffic, saving latency. A common misconception is to treat Exclusive and Shared as interchangeable; they are not. Exclusive encodes the guarantee that no other cache holds the line, and that guarantee is what avoids a BusUpgr or BusRdX for a following write. Think about data structures where a thread reads then writes — E helps those patterns. Key takeaway: states encode ownership and cleanliness. Which threads in your workload will benefit from the Exclusive optimization?

keyIdea.title: State roles
keyIdea.text: M = dirty owner; E = clean exclusive owner; S = clean shared copy; I = invalid. Exclusive avoids write-side bus traffic.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › MESI States
State definitions
M
Modified
Dirty copy, sole valid owner. Memory is stale; writeback required on eviction.
E
Exclusive
Clean and only this cache has it. Can be written locally without bus traffic.
S
Shared
Clean, may be in multiple caches. A write requires invalidation of peers.
I
Invalid
No valid copy locally.
Example
A core reads a block nobody else has. The controller grants E. If the core writes immediately, it transitions to M locally with zero bus traffic — this reduces latency for read-then-write patterns.
Common misconception
Treating E and S as equivalent misses the critical exclusivity guarantee. If a cache believes it is Exclusive when another has a copy, correctness fails. Protocols ensure E only when no sharers exist.
Key Takeaway

Encode ownership separately from cleanliness: Exclusive gives permission to write without announcing it.

screens.title: Processor Actions: PrRd and PrWr Transitions
screens.narratorSegment: Processor actions drive state changes and sometimes bus transactions. On a processor read when the line is Invalid, the cache issues a BusRd. The resulting state becomes Shared if other caches have it, or Exclusive if no other cache responded. On a processor write from Invalid, the cache issues BusRdX and obtains Modified. When the line is Shared and the processor writes, the cache issues BusUpgr to invalidate other sharers and transitions to Modified. When the line is Exclusive and the processor writes, no bus transaction is needed; the cache simply transitions to Modified. For a line in Modified, both reads and writes happen locally and the state remains M. As a concrete walkthrough, consider a core that reads a block it doesn't have: it issues BusRd, gets E if no sharer exists, or S if others do. If it then writes, E→M happens locally. Many engineers misapply BusRdX where BusUpgr suffices: BusRdX fetches exclusive rights and data, while BusUpgr assumes data is already present and only invalidates peers. Remember to choose the lighter-weight BusUpgr when the cache already has a clean copy in S. How would a frequent read-then-write pattern benefit from E grants?

keyIdea.title: Processor-driven rules
keyIdea.text: PrRd from I issues BusRd; PrWr from S issues BusUpgr; E→M needs no bus traffic; writebacks only for M evictions.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Processor Actions
Processor-triggered transitions
PrRd from I: Issue BusRd → result S or E depending on sharers.
PrWr from I: Issue BusRdX → transition to M once exclusive data obtained.
PrWr from S: Issue BusUpgr → invalidate sharers and transition to M.
PrWr from E: No bus transaction → local write, E→M.
PrRd/PrWr from M: Access locally, remain M.
Example
A core that reads a block and later writes it will often see I→E on BusRd and then E→M locally with zero bus traffic. This saves the cost of fetching or invalidating peers.
Common mistake
Issuing BusRdX instead of BusUpgr when the cache already holds a clean shared copy wastes bus bandwidth because BusRdX fetches data and exclusive rights rather than just invalidating peers.
Key Takeaway

Use BusUpgr to upgrade a local shared copy to modified without fetching data; avoid unnecessary BusRdX calls.

screens.title: Bus Actions: BusRd, BusRdX, BusUpgr and Peer Reactions
screens.narratorSegment: Bus transactions mediate sharing between caches. When a cache issues BusRd because it needs a line, other caches respond if they hold the line. A cache in M must write back to memory and transition to S when it supplies data to a BusRd. A cache in E will supply data and transition to S. Shared caches remain S and may supply data. BusRdX, which requests exclusive ownership for a write, forces other S or E caches to invalidate and any M owner to write back and become I. BusUpgr is lighter: it upgrades an existing shared copy to exclusive by invalidating other sharers without fetching data. Consider a sequence where P2 writes a line while P1 and P3 hold shared copies: P2 issues BusUpgr, causing P1 and P3 to invalidate and P2 to become M. A misconception is to expect M to remain unchanged on a peer's BusUpgr; M cannot coexist with another cache's M. Recognize also that supply-from-cache versus memory writeback changes latency: cache-to-cache supply is faster. When a bus request arrives, always ask: does the requester already have the line? If so, upgrade; if not, fetch exclusive with BusRdX. How will these bus choices show up in your coherence traffic measurements?

keyIdea.title: Bus semantics
keyIdea.text: BusRd may cause M→S with a writeback; BusRdX invalidates peers and forces M owners to write back; BusUpgr invalidates without data movement.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Bus Actions
Bus action table (conceptual)
BusRd: Other caches may supply data. M transitions to S and writes back; E becomes S and supplies.
BusRdX: Request exclusive ownership. S/E caches transition to I; M writes back and becomes I after supplying.
BusUpgr: Invalidate other sharers only; no data fetch if requester already has a clean copy.
Example
If P2 issues BusRd and P1 has the block in M, P1 supplies data and writes back to memory, then transitions to S. The requester obtains S. That writeback is the extra memory transaction MESI sometimes triggers.
Misconception
Don't assume BusUpgr moves data. It only invalidates peers when the requester already has the clean copy locally.
Why this matters

Choosing between BusRdX and BusUpgr changes whether data crosses the memory controller. That choice directly affects latency and memory bandwidth under sharing patterns.

screens.title: MESI Optimizations: Silent Evictions and Writebacks
screens.narratorSegment: An important optimization in MESI is the silent eviction of lines in E or S: because memory is up-to-date, evicting these lines need not write back to memory. Only lines in M require a writeback on eviction because they contain modifications not reflected in memory. This behavior reduces unnecessary memory traffic when caches evict clean data. A concrete scenario: a cache holds a line in E and later must evict it to make space for a new block. Because E is clean, the controller can simply discard the block without issuing a writeback. Developers sometimes assume every eviction triggers a memory write, which overestimates traffic. Another subtle point: eviction policies that frequently evict M-state lines will generate writebacks and increase memory bandwidth usage. If your workload creates many short-lived modifications, consider how associativity and capacity influence how often M lines are written back. Key takeaway: only dirty state forces writeback; clean states can be silently discarded. How might this influence your design of cache replacement policies for write-heavy workloads? In practical terms, when an eviction needs no writeback and why only m matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Eviction rule
keyIdea.text: Evicting E or S is silent—no writeback. Only M-state evictions require writing modified data to memory.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Silent Evictions
Silent evictions explained
Lines in E or S are clean: memory already reflects the most recent value, so an eviction does not require a writeback.
Lines in M are dirty: evicting must write the modified data back to memory to preserve correctness.
Replacement policies that evict M frequently increase memory traffic and latency due to writebacks.
Example
A block loaded as E that is later chosen for eviction is simply discarded, saving a memory write. If the block had been modified (M), eviction would produce a writeback to memory.
Impact

Silent evictions reduce write traffic and matter for write-heavy workloads where clean copies are common.

Misconception
Not every eviction writes to memory. Only dirty copies in M cause writebacks.

screens.title: Cache-to-Cache Transfers and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Cache-to-cache transfers occur when a requester finds the data in another cache's M or E state and that cache supplies the data directly, bypassing memory. This is typically faster because the transfer avoids the memory controller latency and possible DRAM access. In MESI, when a cache in M or E receives a BusRd, it can supply the data to the requester—M may also write back to memory in MESI depending on the implementation, but supplying directly remains a lower-latency path. The practical effect is that sharing patterns where a modified block is read by another core shortly after modification benefit from cache-to-cache supply. A concrete example from the chapter: P2 writes A and then P1 reads A; P2 can supply the data on BusRd so P1 receives it quickly. A common misconception is to assume memory is always the canonical fast path; in fact, cache-to-cache traffic is usually shorter in latency. When analyzing performance, count cache-to-cache supplies separately from memory reads and writebacks because they represent saved memory transactions. Key question: for your workload, do modified blocks tend to be read soon by other cores? If yes, enabling cache-to-cache supply or MOESI Owned state can reduce memory traffic and latency.

keyIdea.title: Supply benefits
keyIdea.text: Cache-to-cache supply bypasses memory, reducing latency and memory-controller load when modified or exclusive copies are available in another cache.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Cache-to-Cache Supply
Why it helps
Supplying data from another cache avoids a memory read, typically lowering latency and reducing memory controller load.
When an M or E owner responds to BusRd, the requester can get data faster than fetching from DRAM.
Measure cache-to-cache supplies separately from memory read counts when evaluating protocol performance.
Example scenario
P2 modifies a block, making it M. A subsequent BusRd from P1 can be satisfied by P2 directly, giving P1 a clean copy quickly and reducing memory reads.
Misconception
Assuming memory will always be used to serve requests inflates predicted memory traffic. Cache-to-cache supply is an intended optimization in MESI implementations.
Key Takeaway

Cache-to-cache transfers can significantly reduce memory reads and lower latency when ownership or forwarder responsibilities allow caches to supply data directly.

screens.title: MESIF: The Forward State (F)
screens.narratorSegment: MESIF adds a Forward state to MESI to reduce memory traffic when lines are shared. The Forward state designates one sharer as responsible for answering subsequent read requests for a shared line. When a new cache issues a read for a line that is shared, the forwarder supplies the data instead of the memory controller, reducing load on memory. The forwarder holds a clean copy and, after supplying the data to the new reader, typically transitions to S while the new reader becomes the forwarder. MESIF is valuable in topologies where many caches frequently read the same data: the forwarder eliminates extra memory reads. An example: a line is shared among P1 and P2 with P1 as forwarder. When P3 issues a read, P1 supplies the data, and P1 may remain or revert to S while P3 becomes the forwarder. A common misconception is to assume any sharer can always respond fastest; the forwarder is explicitly chosen to streamline which cache responds. The practical question is whether your platform or workload benefits from a single forwarder — for read-heavy shared data, MESIF can significantly reduce pressure on the memory controller.

keyIdea.title: Forwarder role
keyIdea.text: An F-state cache is a designated sharer that supplies shared clean data to new readers, reducing memory reads.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › MESIF
What is F?
F designates one shared cache as the forwarder responsible for supplying a clean copy to new readers.
Supplying from the forwarder avoids a memory read and reduces pressure on the memory controller.
After forwarding, the forwarder typically transitions to S while the requester becomes the new forwarder.
Example
If P1 is F for a shared line and P3 requests it, P1 supplies the data. Memory is not touched, saving a memory access and lowering latency.
Where used
Intel processors use MESIF to reduce load on the memory controller for read-heavy sharing.
Key Takeaway

Forwarding centralizes response responsibility to one sharer, sparing memory and improving latency for shared reads.

screens.title: MOESI: The Owned (O) State
screens.narratorSegment: MOESI extends MESI with an Owned state to reduce writebacks when a modified line is read by another cache. An Owned line is dirty but shared: one cache retains the dirty copy and is responsible for supplying it to other readers, while memory remains stale. When an M owner receives a BusRd under MOESI, it transitions to O rather than S and keeps the dirty data to serve future requests. This avoids the writeback that MESI typically performs when M transitions to S, saving a memory write followed by a memory read if another cache later requests the line. A concrete example: P2 modifies a block and is M. When P1 issues BusRd, under MESI P2 would write back and become S; under MOESI P2 becomes O, keeps the dirty copy, and supplies P1 directly. The misconception to avoid is believing that dirty sharing always forces memory updates. Owned lets dirty data be shared without immediate memory synchronization. The key question: does your workload have patterns where modified data is then read by other cores? If so, MOESI can reduce memory traffic.

narration.text: MOESI extends MESI with an Owned state to reduce writebacks when a modified line is read by another cache. An Owned line is dirty but shared: one cache retains the dirty copy and is responsible for supplying it to other readers, while memory remains stale. When an M owner receives a BusRd under MOESI, it transitions to O rather than S and keeps the dirty data to serve future requests. This avoids the writeback that MESI typically performs when M transitions to S, saving a memory write followed by a memory read if another cache later requests the line. A concrete example: P2 modifies a block and is M. When P1 issues BusRd, under MESI P2 would write back and become S; under MOESI P2 becomes O, keeps the dirty copy, and supplies P1 directly. The misconception to avoid is believing that dirty sharing always forces memory updates. Owned lets dirty data be shared without immediate memory synchronization. The key question: does your workload have patterns where modified data is then read by other cores? If so, MOESI can reduce memory traffic.

screens.title: MESI vs MESIF vs MOESI
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing MESI, MESIF and MOESI highlights different strategies to reduce memory input and output. MESI provides the baseline four-state protocol with cache-to-cache supply but may perform a writeback when M transitions to S. MESIF adds a Forward state so one sharer supplies data to new readers, reducing memory reads for clean shared lines. MOESI adds Owned so a dirty shareable copy can be retained by a cache and supplied to peers without a writeback. Consider the trade-offs: MESIF centralizes response responsibility and lowers memory-controller load for read-heavy sharing, but requires tracking a forwarder. MOESI avoids some writebacks but requires keeping track of ownership and ensuring the owner supplies dirty data correctly. A common misconception is that either extension is universally best; the advantage depends on workload patterns. For read-heavy read-sharing, MESIF reduces controller reads. For workloads with modified data followed by reads, MOESI reduces writebacks. When you evaluate a protocol, measure actual memory reads and writebacks for your workload to quantify the gains. screens.title: Coherence Traffic Analysis: a 3-cache Sequence
screens.narratorSegment: Let's analyze the example sequence from the chapter and count coherence events. The sequence is: P1: Read A; P2: Read A; P3: Read A; P2: Write A; P1: Read A. Step by step: P1 reads A from memory — BusRd — and gets E because no other caches had it. P2 reads A — BusRd — P1 transitions to S and P2 gets S. P3 reads A — BusRd — another shared copy is created; either memory or an existing sharer supplies data. P2 writes A — PrWr from S issues BusUpgr and transitions P2 to M while invalidating P1 and P3. P1 then reads A — BusRd — P2 supplies data. Under MESI, when P2 supplies data on that BusRd it transitions from M to S and writes back to memory, producing a writeback. Under MOESI, P2 transitions from M to O and supplies the dirty copy without writing back, avoiding the memory writeback. The coherence traffic counted is three bus requests (BusRd, BusUpgr, BusRd) and one writeback in MESI but zero writebacks in MOESI for the final supply. This example shows how Owned avoids a writeback by keeping the dirty owner responsible for supply. A useful reflective question is: which workloads cause many such transitions, and how often will Owned save a writeback?

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a clear, practical understanding of cache coherence protocols used in shared-memory multiprocessors. You will learn the MESI protocol's four states, how processor reads and writes trigger state transitions, and how bus transactions such as BusRd, BusRdX and BusUpgr coordinate consistency. We'll also examine MESIF's forwarding optimization and MOESI's Owned state, both designed to reduce memory traffic by enabling cache-to-cache transfers or allowing a dirty copy to be shared. As you follow the chapter, you'll see concrete examples of state transitions, observe the coherence traffic produced by simple read-write sequences, and practice a short simulation comparing MESI and MOESI. Understanding these mechanisms matters because coherence traffic often becomes a performance bottleneck in multicore systems. By the end, you'll be able to reason about when a forwarder or an owned copy saves time and when BusUpgr avoids unnecessary data movement. Which part of the protocol do you expect will make the largest difference in your workloads?

By the end of this chapter you should be able to implement MESI state transitions, explain and compare MESIF and MOESI, and analyze coherence traffic for common access patterns. First, you will learn to map processor reads and writes to state changes and the bus operations they trigger, which is essential to reason about correctness and performance. Second, you will understand MESIF's forwarding and MOESI's Owned state and when each reduces memory input and output. Third, you will be able to trace cache-to-cache transfers and count bus transactions for a sequence of operations, identifying where writebacks occur. Finally, you'll apply these skills to a short simulation that contrasts MESI and MOESI and shows how an Owned state can eliminate writebacks during sharing of modified data. These objectives are practical: they let you predict when memory controller load grows and how protocol choices change latency. Think of these skills as tools you can use to evaluate architectures or tune software sharing patterns to reduce coherence overhead.

These objectives focus on practical skills you can evidence quickly. You should be able to draw state-transition diagrams for MESI and annotate them for both processor and bus events. You should be able to describe when a BusUpgr is sufficient versus when a BusRdX is required, and explain why E-to-M needs no bus transaction. You will practice tracing cache-to-cache transfers so you can count saved memory reads and writebacks. Finally, you will compare the coherence traffic of MESI, MESIF and MOESI for a short sequence of reads and writes. Being able to quantify transactions matters because architecture choices and workload patterns have measurable effects on latency and bandwidth usage. For instance, knowing that a forwarder in MESIF can supply a shared line spares a memory read helps you predict benefits for read-heavy sharing. As you practice, record the bus events and ask which optimization gives the most savings for your target workload.

Let's define each MESI state and connect it to correctness and performance. Modified means the cache line has been changed and memory is stale; this cache is the sole valid source. Exclusive means the cache has a clean copy and no other cache has it — the cache can promote to modified without notifying the bus. Shared means the line is clean and may be present in multiple caches; after a write, those other copies must be invalidated. Invalid means the line is not valid locally. These four states let caches avoid unnecessary traffic: E allows a write without a bus transaction, and S lets multiple readers avoid coordination. A concrete example: a core that reads a block and then writes it alone will often get E and then go to M with no bus traffic, saving latency. A common misconception is to treat Exclusive and Shared as interchangeable; they are not. Exclusive encodes the guarantee that no other cache holds the line, and that guarantee is what avoids a BusUpgr or BusRdX for a following write. Think about data structures where a thread reads then writes — E helps those patterns. Key takeaway: states encode ownership and cleanliness. Which threads in your workload will benefit from the Exclusive optimization?

Processor actions drive state changes and sometimes bus transactions. On a processor read when the line is Invalid, the cache issues a BusRd. The resulting state becomes Shared if other caches have it, or Exclusive if no other cache responded. On a processor write from Invalid, the cache issues BusRdX and obtains Modified. When the line is Shared and the processor writes, the cache issues BusUpgr to invalidate other sharers and transitions to Modified. When the line is Exclusive and the processor writes, no bus transaction is needed; the cache simply transitions to Modified. For a line in Modified, both reads and writes happen locally and the state remains M. As a concrete walkthrough, consider a core that reads a block it doesn't have: it issues BusRd, gets E if no sharer exists, or S if others do. If it then writes, E→M happens locally. Many engineers misapply BusRdX where BusUpgr suffices: BusRdX fetches exclusive rights and data, while BusUpgr assumes data is already present and only invalidates peers. Remember to choose the lighter-weight BusUpgr when the cache already has a clean copy in S. How would a frequent read-then-write pattern benefit from E grants?

Bus transactions mediate sharing between caches. When a cache issues BusRd because it needs a line, other caches respond if they hold the line. A cache in M must write back to memory and transition to S when it supplies data to a BusRd. A cache in E will supply data and transition to S. Shared caches remain S and may supply data. BusRdX, which requests exclusive ownership for a write, forces other S or E caches to invalidate and any M owner to write back and become I. BusUpgr is lighter: it upgrades an existing shared copy to exclusive by invalidating other sharers without fetching data. Consider a sequence where P2 writes a line while P1 and P3 hold shared copies: P2 issues BusUpgr, causing P1 and P3 to invalidate and P2 to become M. A misconception is to expect M to remain unchanged on a peer's BusUpgr; M cannot coexist with another cache's M. Recognize also that supply-from-cache versus memory writeback changes latency: cache-to-cache supply is faster. When a bus request arrives, always ask: does the requester already have the line? If so, upgrade; if not, fetch exclusive with BusRdX. How will these bus choices show up in your coherence traffic measurements?

An important optimization in MESI is the silent eviction of lines in E or S: because memory is up-to-date, evicting these lines need not write back to memory. Only lines in M require a writeback on eviction because they contain modifications not reflected in memory. This behavior reduces unnecessary memory traffic when caches evict clean data. A concrete scenario: a cache holds a line in E and later must evict it to make space for a new block. Because E is clean, the controller can simply discard the block without issuing a writeback. Developers sometimes assume every eviction triggers a memory write, which overestimates traffic. Another subtle point: eviction policies that frequently evict M-state lines will generate writebacks and increase memory bandwidth usage. If your workload creates many short-lived modifications, consider how associativity and capacity influence how often M lines are written back. Key takeaway: only dirty state forces writeback; clean states can be silently discarded. How might this influence your design of cache replacement policies for write-heavy workloads? MESI Optimizations: Silent Evictions and Writebacks means evicting e or s is silent—no writeback. only m-state evictions require writing modified data to memory.. In practical terms, when an eviction needs no writeback and why only m matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cache-to-cache transfers occur when a requester finds the data in another cache's M or E state and that cache supplies the data directly, bypassing memory. This is typically faster because the transfer avoids the memory controller latency and possible DRAM access. In MESI, when a cache in M or E receives a BusRd, it can supply the data to the requester—M may also write back to memory in MESI depending on the implementation, but supplying directly remains a lower-latency path. The practical effect is that sharing patterns where a modified block is read by another core shortly after modification benefit from cache-to-cache supply. A concrete example from the chapter: P2 writes A and then P1 reads A; P2 can supply the data on BusRd so P1 receives it quickly. A common misconception is to assume memory is always the canonical fast path; in fact, cache-to-cache traffic is usually shorter in latency. When analyzing performance, count cache-to-cache supplies separately from memory reads and writebacks because they represent saved memory transactions. Key question: for your workload, do modified blocks tend to be read soon by other cores? If yes, enabling cache-to-cache supply or MOESI Owned state can reduce memory traffic and latency.

MESIF adds a Forward state to MESI to reduce memory traffic when lines are shared. The Forward state designates one sharer as responsible for answering subsequent read requests for a shared line. When a new cache issues a read for a line that is shared, the forwarder supplies the data instead of the memory controller, reducing load on memory. The forwarder holds a clean copy and, after supplying the data to the new reader, typically transitions to S while the new reader becomes the forwarder. MESIF is valuable in topologies where many caches frequently read the same data: the forwarder eliminates extra memory reads. An example: a line is shared among P1 and P2 with P1 as forwarder. When P3 issues a read, P1 supplies the data, and P1 may remain or revert to S while P3 becomes the forwarder. A common misconception is to assume any sharer can always respond fastest; the forwarder is explicitly chosen to streamline which cache responds. The practical question is whether your platform or workload benefits from a single forwarder — for read-heavy shared data, MESIF can significantly reduce pressure on the memory controller.

MOESI extends MESI with an Owned state to reduce writebacks when a modified line is read by another cache. An Owned line is dirty but shared: one cache retains the dirty copy and is responsible for supplying it to other readers, while memory remains stale. When an M owner receives a BusRd under MOESI, it transitions to O rather than S and keeps the dirty data to serve future requests. This avoids the writeback that MESI typically performs when M transitions to S, saving a memory write followed by a memory read if another cache later requests the line. A concrete example: P2 modifies a block and is M. When P1 issues BusRd, under MESI P2 would write back and become S; under MOESI P2 becomes O, keeps the dirty copy, and supplies P1 directly. The misconception to avoid is believing that dirty sharing always forces memory updates. Owned lets dirty data be shared without immediate memory synchronization. The key question: does your workload have patterns where modified data is then read by other cores? If so, MOESI can reduce memory traffic.

Comparing MESI, MESIF and MOESI highlights different strategies to reduce memory input and output. MESI provides the baseline four-state protocol with cache-to-cache supply but may perform a writeback when M transitions to S. MESIF adds a Forward state so one sharer supplies data to new readers, reducing memory reads for clean shared lines. MOESI adds Owned so a dirty shareable copy can be retained by a cache and supplied to peers without a writeback. Consider the trade-offs: MESIF centralizes response responsibility and lowers memory-controller load for read-heavy sharing, but requires tracking a forwarder. MOESI avoids some writebacks but requires keeping track of ownership and ensuring the owner supplies dirty data correctly. A common misconception is that either extension is universally best; the advantage depends on workload patterns. For read-heavy read-sharing, MESIF reduces controller reads. For workloads with modified data followed by reads, MOESI reduces writebacks. When you evaluate a protocol, measure actual memory reads and writebacks for your workload to quantify the gains. Which protocol would you choose if your workload often modifies data then has many readers afterwards? MESI vs MESIF vs MOESI means mesif reduces memory reads via a forwarder; moesi reduces writebacks via an owned dirty sharer. the right choice depends on sharing patterns.. In practical terms, trade-offs: forwarding, owned copies, and memory traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's analyze the example sequence from the chapter and count coherence events. The sequence is: P1: Read A; P2: Read A; P3: Read A; P2: Write A; P1: Read A. Step by step: P1 reads A from memory — BusRd — and gets E because no other caches had it. P2 reads A — BusRd — P1 transitions to S and P2 gets S. P3 reads A — BusRd — another shared copy is created; either memory or an existing sharer supplies data. P2 writes A — PrWr from S issues BusUpgr and transitions P2 to M while invalidating P1 and P3. P1 then reads A — BusRd — P2 supplies data. Under MESI, when P2 supplies data on that BusRd it transitions from M to S and writes back to memory, producing a writeback. Under MOESI, P2 transitions from M to O and supplies the dirty copy without writing back, avoiding the memory writeback. The coherence traffic counted is three bus requests (BusRd, BusUpgr, BusRd) and one writeback in MESI but zero writebacks in MOESI for the final supply. This example shows how Owned avoids a writeback by keeping the dirty owner responsible for supply. A useful reflective question is: which workloads cause many such transitions, and how often will Owned save a writeback?

Now practice the hands-on simulation from the chapter. The trace is: P1: Read 0x1000; P2: Read 0x1000; P3: Write 0x1000; P1: Read 0x1000; P2: Write 0x1000; P3: Read 0x1000. Step through each access and record the local state change and any bus transaction. For MESI, start with all caches I and memory holding the block. P1's initial read issues BusRd and becomes E. P2's read issues BusRd, causing P1 to transition to S and P2 to S. P3's write from S will issue BusUpgr and transition P3 to M while invalidating others. When P1 reads again, it issues BusRd and P3 supplies data; under MESI P3 transitions to S and writes back to memory. Continue the trace for the remaining steps and tally BusRd, BusUpgr, BusRdX, and writebacks. For MOESI repeat the same sequence; when P3 supplies the dirty data on a BusRd it transitions to O rather than performing a writeback, and later supplies remain cache-to-cache. The important result to observe is how many writebacks occur under MESI versus MOESI and how many bus transactions are shared supplies versus memory accesses. After completing your trace, ask: how many writebacks did MOESI save compared to MESI for this workload?

Summarizing the chapter: remember the MESI states — Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid — and that E lets a cache write locally without a bus transaction. Bus actions BusRd, BusRdX and BusUpgr coordinate data supply and invalidations; use BusUpgr to upgrade a local shared copy to modified when you already have clean data. Cache-to-cache transfers and MESIF's Forward state reduce memory reads by having a sharer supply data. MOESI's Owned state avoids writebacks by letting a dirty owner supply data to readers without writing back to memory. Silent evictions only apply to clean states; only M requires writeback on eviction. When analyzing coherence traffic, count bus transactions and writebacks separately to see where protocol extensions save memory input and output. Finally, apply these insights by tracing real sequences; the hands-on simulation shows how MOESI can eliminate writebacks for modified-then-shared patterns. Which optimization matters most depends on whether your workload is read-shared or dirty-then-read shared.

Keep three simple reminders in mind as you work with coherence protocols. First, Exclusive is not Shared: E grants the right to write locally without a bus transaction, so it avoids upgrades. Second, choose BusUpgr when you already have a clean shared copy to avoid unnecessary fetching; BusRdX is heavier. Third, protocol extensions target different problems: MESIF reduces memory reads with a forwarder, MOESI reduces writebacks with an Owned dirty sharer. When profiling, record BusRd, BusRdX, BusUpgr counts and writebacks. These metrics reveal which optimization will provide real benefit for your workload. Finally, always trace a small sequence to validate assumptions — seeing the state transitions makes the trade-offs concrete.
